newsitem.title: GERMANY: Bonn urges building sector to accept pay deal.
newsitem.headline: Bonn urges building sector to accept pay deal.

text.p: The German government on Friday urged the construction industry union and employers to accept a controversial wage deal proposal and warned that a strike would be "poison" for the troubled sector.

Construction minister Klaus Toepfer said the agreement, which cuts sick pay by 20 percent and raises wages by less than the rate of inflation, was "socially acceptable and economically sensible" given current conditions in the sector.

He noted that new building orders in Germany had fallen by 8.7 percent in January and February. "If I look at that then a labour dispute in such a situation would of course be poison," Toepfer said in a radio interview.
The agreement, reached in the early hours of Thursday after 20 hours of arbitration talks, falls far short of what the two sides were demanding and has yet to be ratified by their respective boards.

If the deal is not approved by May 21, the IG Bau union can lawfully call industrial action. The union's wages commission will meet on Monday to discuss the pact and will hold a news conference at 1200 GMT.

Analysts believe any strike is likely to be limited since neither side can afford a prolonged dispute in a sector suffering from mass unemployment, with about 400,000 of its 1.3 million workers out of a job.
The industry, seen as having the highest costs in the world, is suffering from a surplus of capacity now that the east German building boom which followed unification in 1990 has fizzled out.
"Any strike would definitely not be a long one," said Uwe Weinreich, construction analyst at BHF-Bank. "Both sides would be forced to find a solution quickly."

Under the proposed deal, workers' pay will be cut by 20 percent during the first three weeks of sickness, wages will be raised by 1.3 percent from last April 1 and Christmas bonuses will also be cut. German inflation stands at about 1.5 percent.
The IG Bau union had, among other demands, called for wage increase of 2.9 percent and continued full pay during sick leave while employers had sought to keep pay unchanged.
The agreement, brokered by Heiner Geissler, a senior politician from Chancellor Helmut Kohl's Christian Democrats, also allows the long-term unemployed to be hired at lower starting wages.
In addition, the Christmas bonus or so-called "13th month" salary will be cut to about 77 percent of a month's salary.
Officials on both sides are sceptical whether the leadership of the industry employer group or IG Bau will approve the deal, which was reached by just five votes to four.
Two representatives from the employers and two from IG Bau voted against it. IG Bau leader Klaus Wiesenhuegel said he was concerned the reduced sick-pay benefits would be rejected by union members.
Analysts said the deal had a better chance of being accepted in west Germany, than in the former communist east, where wages are still below west German levels.
Geissler said in a radio interview on Friday a collapse "would be the worst that could happen to the construction sector."
He said he feared the deal may be rejected but added that negotiators could not have achieved a better one as tens of thousands of small firms were already in financial trouble.
